los.text: Take a focused history from a patient and explain health risks associated with pre-diabetes.
sessions: Obesity history with BMI calculation - dealing with sensitive issues
los.html:
• Focused history: symptoms of diabetes (thirst, polyuria, tiredness, recurrent infections, blurred vision)
    • weight history
    • diet
    • physical activity
    • alcohol
    • smoking
    • family history of diabetes and heart disease
    • previous gestational diabetes
    • medications (steroids, antipsychotics)
    • ethnicity (South Asian, Black African/Caribbean: higher risk).
Pre-diabetes (non-diabetic hyperglycaemia)
HbA1c 42–47 mmol/mol or fasting glucose 5.5–6.9 mmol/L
Risks: type 2 diabetes (about 5–10% per year), cardiovascular disease, stroke
Reversible: weight loss of 5–10%, 150 min/week activity, diet → NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme
Review HbA1c yearly
  • Explain: chunk and check, plain language, link risks to their own goals.

los.text: Discuss a patient’s weight with confidence and sensitivity, using appropriate communication strategies.
sessions: Obesity history with BMI calculation - dealing with sensitive issues
los.html:
DoAvoid
Ask permission: "Would it be OK to talk about your weight today?"Blaming or judging
Use neutral words ("weight", "BMI")Labels like "obese" without care
Explore their views, previous attempts, barriersAssuming they lack motivation
Focus on health goals they care aboutLecturing
Offer specific support (referral, programmes)Vague advice
  • Very brief advice model works: ask, advise, act/assist.

los.text: Accurately calculate a patient’s Body Mass Index (BMI) using standard formulae
sessions: Obesity history with BMI calculation - dealing with sensitive issues
los.html:
• BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height (m)². Example: 95 kg, 1.75 m → 95 ÷ 3.06 = 31.0 kg/m².
BMICategory (adults)
<18.5Underweight
18.5–24.9Healthy
25–29.9Overweight
30–34.9Obesity class I
35–39.9Obesity class II
≥40Obesity class III
  • Lower thresholds (by 2.5) for South Asian, Chinese, Black African and Caribbean people (NICE).
  • Limitations: muscular people, older people, pregnancy; add waist circumference or waist-to-height ratio (keep below 0.5).

los.text: Perform a competent cardiovascular examination with increased confidence
los.html:
• Full routine: see ICM Year 1 › Cardiovascular › LO 1.
Fluency points
Palpate the apex beat and describe its position by intercostal space and line
Time murmurs with the carotid pulse (systolic coincides with the pulse)
Use positional manoeuvres when a murmur is suspected
Always check lung bases and peripheral oedema

los.text: Interpret basic clinical signs identified during a cardiovascular examination.
los.html:
FindingInterpretation
Irregularly irregular pulseAtrial fibrillation
Slow-rising pulse, ejection systolic murmur radiating to carotidsAortic stenosis
Collapsing pulse, early diastolic murmur (sitting forward)Aortic regurgitation
Pansystolic murmur at apex radiating to axillaMitral regurgitation
Mid-diastolic rumble at apex (bell, left lateral)Mitral stenosis
Displaced apexLV dilatation (heart failure, regurgitation)
Raised JVP, ankle oedema, basal cracklesHeart failure / fluid overload
Sternotomy scar, metallic clickPrevious CABG / valve replacement
Splinter haemorrhages, new murmur, feverInfective endocarditis

los.text: Describe the stages of a rapid assessment of a sick patient and identify appropriate interventions
sessions: A to E assessment of the sick patient
los.html:
StageLook forInterventions
AirwayTalking? Stridor, gurgling, obstructionHead tilt/chin lift, suction, adjuncts, call anaesthetist
BreathingRR, sats, effort, chest examOxygen, nebulisers, ABG, CXR
CirculationHR, BP, CRT, JVP, heart sounds, urine outputIV access, bloods (incl. cultures, lactate), fluid bolus 500 mL, ECG, catheter
DisabilityACVPU/GCS, pupils, glucose, temperatureTreat hypoglycaemia, analgesia
ExposureRashes, bleeding, calves, abdomen, woundsTreat the cause
  • Principles: treat problems as you find them before moving on
    • reassess after each intervention
    • call for help early
    • use SBAR to escalate.

los.text: Perform a systematic A to E (Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure) assessment of a sick patient.
sessions: A to E assessment of the sick patient
los.html:
1Approach safely, introduce yourself, ask "How are you?" (a reply shows the airway is open and brain perfused).
2Call for help if very unwell; attach monitoring (sats, BP, ECG).
3Work through A → B → C → D → E, treating as you go.
4Reassess after each intervention and regularly.
5Escalate with SBAR, document, and agree a plan (including ceilings of care).

SiteNotes
Deltoid2–3 finger-breadths below the acromion; small volumes (vaccines)
Vastus lateralisMiddle third of the anterolateral thigh; preferred in infants
Ventrogluteal
  • Gluteus medius (hand on greater trochanter, fingers to ASIS and iliac crest)
  • Preferred for adults for larger volumes, away from nerves and vessels
DorsoglutealUpper outer quadrant of the buttock; avoided now (sciatic nerve, superior gluteal vessels)

los.text: Demonstrate the correct technique for administering an intramuscular injection in a clinical setting.
los.html:
1Check prescription (5 rights), allergies, identity, consent, explain.
2
  • Hand hygiene, ANTT tray
  • Draw up with a drawing-up needle, change to an injection needle (usually 23G, length for the site and body size).
3Expose and locate the site; clean if local policy (allow to dry).
4Stretch the skin (or Z-track technique: pull the skin 2–3 cm sideways), insert the needle at 90° with a quick dart, leaving a third of the shaft out.
5Aspirate if policy (e.g. dorsogluteal), inject slowly (~1 mL per 10 s), wait 10 s, withdraw, release the skin.
6Sharps in the bin immediately, don't massage; check for reactions; document (drug, dose, site, time, batch).

los.text: Demonstrate knowledge of appropriate volume limits for different intramuscular injection sites.
los.html:
SiteMaximum volume (adult, guide)
Deltoid1 mL (up to 2 mL)
Vastus lateralis5 mL (infants 0.5–1 mL)
Ventrogluteal2.5–3 mL (up to 5 mL)
Dorsogluteal3–5 mL (avoid)
  • Larger volumes: split between sites.

los.text: Identify common sites for the administration of subcutaneous injections.
los.html:
SiteNotes
Abdomen~5 cm (two finger-breadths) away from the umbilicus; most common for insulin and LMWH
Outer upper armBack of the arm
Anterior/lateral thigh
Upper buttock
  • Rotate sites to avoid lipohypertrophy (lumpy fat: erratic insulin absorption).

los.text: Demonstrate the correct technique for administering a subcutaneous injection in a clinical setting.
los.html:
1Check prescription, allergies, identity, consent, explain.
2ANTT: hand hygiene, clean tray, protect key parts.
3Pinch a fold of skin (pinch-up), insert the needle at 45–90° depending on needle length and fat (prefilled LMWH: 90° into the pinched fold; don't expel the air bubble in LMWH syringes).
4Inject slowly, hold for ~10 s (insulin pens), withdraw, release the fold.
5Don't rub (bruising with heparin); sharps in the bin; document site, time, dose.

los.text: Demonstrate knowledge of ANTT principles whilst administering an injection
los.html:
ANTT principleIn injections
Hand hygieneBefore and after, and before gloving
Identify key partsNeedle, syringe tip, inside of caps, vial bung
Protect key partsDon't touch; use a non-touch technique; keep on a clean surface
Key siteSkin puncture site: clean if policy, don't re-touch
Aseptic fieldClean tray or general aseptic field
Non-sterile glovesWhere touching blood or risk of exposure
